summary.text: An algal bloom is a rapid rise in the number of algae in fresh water or the sea, often spotted because the water changes colour.
Blooms start when a nutrient the algae need, usually nitrogen or phosphorus, gets into the water, for example in fertilizer runoff.
Each alga lives only a short time, and as decomposers break down the dead ones they use up dissolved oxygen, so fish and other life can die in large numbers.

facts.label: Possible colours
facts.value: Green, red, brown, golden or purple

facts.label: Aquarium cause
facts.value: Overfed fish, with nutrients plants don't absorb

items.prompt: Heavy rain falls on a freshly fertilized field beside a lake. Weeks later the lake turns bright green. What most likely happened?

options.label: The cold rain killed off the lake's fish
Washed-in nutrients made algae multiply fast
The fertilizer chemicals dyed the water green
Soil from the field settled on the surface

items.explain: Runoff carries nutrients such as nitrogen or phosphorus into the water, and algae respond with a burst of growth that colours the water.

items.prompt: A large bloom dies off, and a few days later the water has little oxygen left. Why?

options.label: Dead algae turn the oxygen into toxins
The floating mat stops rain from reaching it
Algae give off a gas that pushes oxygen out
Decomposers breaking down dead algae use it up

items.explain: The short-lived algae leave lots of dead matter, and the decomposers that break it down consume dissolved oxygen as they work.

items.prompt: Your fish tank turns cloudy green after weeks of giving the fish extra food. What is the sensible fix?

options.label: Change the water and feed the fish less
Add more food so the fish eat the algae
Move the tank into brighter sunlight
Keep the water exactly as it is

items.explain: Overfeeding leaves excess nutrients that feed a bloom; changing the water and cutting back on food removes the cause.

items.prompt: Algae are often blamed for spoiling water. Roughly how much of Earth's oxygen do they produce?

options.label: About 5%
About 20%
About 70%
About 95%

items.explain: Algae produce about 70% of Earth's oxygen, which supports life on land.

items.prompt: A city beside a lake shuts off its tap water during a large bloom. What is the likely reason?

options.label: The algae make the water too salty to drink
Bloom water holds far too much oxygen
The algae lower the lake below the pipes
Some bloom algae release toxins into the water

items.explain: Depending on the organism, a bloom can release toxins, and such harmful blooms can lead cities to cut off water to residents.

items.prompt: A remote mountain lake with no farms, towns or sewage nearby has an algal bloom. What does this show?

options.label: Someone must have dumped fertilizer in it
Blooms can occur without human pollution
It must really be a kelp forest instead
Only salt water can bloom without people

items.explain: Freshwater blooms are not always caused by human contamination and have been seen to occur naturally in lakes.

paragraphs.heading: What a bloom is
paragraphs.text: An algal bloom is a fast rise or buildup in the number of algae living in fresh water or the sea. Algae is a broad word for many kinds of water organisms that make food from light, from large seaweeds to single cells such as cyanobacteria. When people say bloom, they usually mean the tiny single-celled kinds, though a kelp forest counts as a bloom of large algae. A bloom is often spotted because the water changes colour.

paragraphs.heading: What sets one off
paragraphs.text: A bloom starts when a nutrient that the algae need reaches the water. That nutrient is usually nitrogen or phosphorus, but it can also be iron, vitamins or amino acids. In the open ocean and along coasts, upwelling driven by winds and by the shape of the seafloor can lift nutrients into the photic zone, the sunlit top layer of the sea. Near coasts and in fresh water, runoff from farms, cities and sewage can do the same job. Once the nutrient arrives, the algae grow much faster than normal.

paragraphs.heading: Colours in the water
paragraphs.text: Blooms can make water less clear and change its colour. The colour comes from pigments inside the algal cells, such as chlorophyll and pigments that protect the cell from light. Depending on the organism, its pigments and how deep it sits, a bloom may look green, red, brown, golden or purple. Bright green blooms in fresh water are often cyanobacteria, nicknamed blue-green algae, such as Microcystis.

paragraphs.heading: How a bloom uses up oxygen
paragraphs.text: Algae multiply quickly when nutrients are plentiful, but each one lives only a short time, so dead material piles up and begins to rot. Decomposers in the water break down the dead algae and use up dissolved oxygen as they do it. Oxygen can then drop sharply, and without enough of it, animals and plants may die in large numbers. Such an area may be called a dead zone. This chain, from too many nutrients to algae growth to lost oxygen, is called eutrophication.

paragraphs.heading: Helpful or harmful
paragraphs.text: A bloom may be harmless or harmful. A small bloom can help the whole ecosystem by feeding other organisms. The effects range from feeding animals higher in the food chain to blocking sunlight, draining oxygen and, for some organisms, releasing toxins. Blooms that injure animals or the environment, especially toxic ones, are called harmful algal blooms, or HABs. They can cause fish die-offs, force cities to shut off residents' water, or make states close fisheries.

paragraphs.heading: A bloom in a fish tank
paragraphs.text: Blooms can appear in freshwater aquariums when fish are given too much food and plants do not take up the extra nutrients. These blooms are usually bad for the fish. The fix is to change the tank's water and then feed less. In lakes and other fresh waters, blooms are not always caused by people, though. They have been seen forming naturally in eutrophic lakes, which are rich in nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphates, and in oligotrophic lakes, which hold little of them.
